text:
Here’s a concise overview of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), also called Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME):

1. Core features  
   • Debilitating fatigue lasting ≥ 6 months, not explained by other medical or psychiatric conditions and not substantially relieved by rest.  
   • Post-exertional malaise (PEM): a prolonged worsening of symptoms after even minor physical or mental activity.  
   • Non-restorative sleep.

2. Other common symptoms  
   • Cognitive difficulties (“brain fog”)—memory lapses, slow information processing.  
   • Orthostatic intolerance—dizziness or light-headedness when standing.  
   • Muscle or joint pain, headaches, sore throat, tender lymph nodes, heightened sensitivity to light/sound, gastrointestinal issues.

3. Possible causes (still under study)  
   • Post-infectious triggers (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus, COVID-19)  
   • Immune-system dysregulation  
   • Autonomic-nervous-system dysfunction  
   • Hormonal and metabolic abnormalities  
   • Genetic susceptibility

4. Diagnosis  
   • No single lab test; it is a clinical diagnosis.  
   • Detailed history, physical exam, and tests to rule out anemia, thyroid disorders, sleep apnea, depression, etc.  
   • Common criteria: Institute of Medicine (IOM) 2015 or Canadian Consensus Criteria.

5. Management (individualized; aims at symptom control)  
   • Activity pacing & energy management (“spoon theory,” heart-rate–based pacing).  
   • Sleep hygiene; address co-existing sleep disorders.  
   • Medications for pain, orthostatic symptoms (e.g., fludrocortisone, midodrine), or co-morbid depression/anxiety where appropriate.  
   • Graded exercise therapy is controversial; many guidelines now advise against fixed exercise programs that risk worsening PEM.  
   • Cognitive-behavioral therapy may help some patients cope but should not be presented as a cure.  
   • Nutrition: balanced diet, adequate hydration; address deficiencies (vitamin B12, D, iron).  
   • Supportive measures: compression garments for orthostatic intolerance, blue-light–blocking glasses for photophobia.  
   • Patient education and psychosocial support—support groups, counseling.  
   • Regular follow-up to reassess symptoms and adjust plan.

6. Prognosis  
   • Course is variable: some improve over time; others remain moderately to severely ill.  
   • Early diagnosis, pacing, and symptom-targeted therapy can improve quality of life, though a definitive cure is not yet available.  
   • Research into antivirals, immunomodulators, and metabolic therapies is ongoing.

7. When to seek immediate medical attention  
   • Rapid worsening of neurological symptoms (e.g., sudden weakness, confusion).  
   • Unexplained weight loss, new cardiac or respiratory symptoms, or severe orthostatic intolerance (fainting).

Always consult a qualified healthcare professional for personalized evaluation and treatment.

text:
Here is a more in-depth overview of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), also called Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME):

1. What it is  
   • A long-term, multisystem illness whose core feature is profound, disabling fatigue that lasts at least 6 months, is not substantially improved by rest, and is severe enough to reduce previous levels of activity.  
   • The term ME/CFS is often used because many patients also experience muscle pain (myalgia) and signs of neurologic or immunologic dysfunction (encephalomyelitis).

2. Key symptoms  
   • Post-exertional malaise (PEM): a flare-up of all symptoms after even mild mental or physical effort.  
   • Unrefreshing sleep.  
   • Cognitive problems (“brain fog”) such as slowed thinking, memory lapses, or difficulty concentrating.  
   • Orthostatic intolerance: feeling light-headed or faint when standing or sitting upright.  
   • Muscle or joint pain, headaches, sore throat, and tender lymph nodes are also common.

3. Possible causes (still under study)  
   • Viral or other infections (e.g., Epstein–Barr virus, COVID-19).  
   • Immune system abnormalities.  
   • Hormonal or autonomic-nervous-system dysregulation.  
   • Genetic susceptibility.  
   No single cause has been proven; it is likely multifactorial.

4. Diagnosis  
   • There is no single diagnostic test. Doctors rule out other conditions (e.g., anemia, thyroid disease, depression) through history, exam, and lab tests.  
   • Several clinical criteria sets exist; the U.S. CDC now follows the 2015 Institute of Medicine criteria emphasizing 6-month fatigue, PEM, unrefreshing sleep, and either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance.

5. Treatment and management  
   • No cure yet, so treatment focuses on symptom control and activity management.  
   • Pacing: planning activities and rest to avoid triggering PEM.  
   • Sleep hygiene techniques or sleep medications if needed.  
   • Medications for pain, orthostatic intolerance (e.g., fludrocortisone, midodrine), or comorbid depression/anxiety.  
   • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and supportive counseling can help with coping skills, though they do not cure the illness.  
   • Gentle, patient-led graded activity only if tolerated; many people cannot increase exercise without worsening symptoms.  
   • Address co-existing conditions such as fibromyalgia, migraine, or irritable bowel syndrome.

6. Prognosis  
   • Course is variable. Some improve significantly, especially within the first few years; others experience relapsing or persistent symptoms.  
   • Complete recovery is uncommon but not impossible. Early recognition and appropriate pacing appear to improve outlook.

7. When to see a healthcare professional  
   • Persistent, unexplained fatigue lasting longer than a few months.  
   • Worsening exercise intolerance, cognitive problems, or sleep issues.  
   Early evaluation can exclude other treatable disorders and start supportive care sooner.

8. Self-care tips  
   • Keep a symptom and activity diary to identify personal PEM triggers.  
   • Prioritize restful sleep environment.  
   • Maintain balanced nutrition; small, frequent meals sometimes help with orthostatic symptoms.  
   • Join a support group (in-person or online) for practical coping strategies.

9. Resources  
   • U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): cdc.gov/me-cfs  
   • ME Association (UK): meassociation.org.uk  
   • Solve ME/CFS Initiative (USA): solveme.org

If you need more detail—such as specific medication options, how to implement pacing, or guidance on finding an ME/CFS-aware clinician—just let me know.

1. Core features  
   • Debilitating fatigue lasting at least 6 months that is not significantly improved by rest and not explained by other medical conditions.  
   • Post-exertional malaise (marked worsening of symptoms after physical or mental activity that can last days or weeks).  
   • Unrefreshing sleep.  
   • Cognitive problems (“brain fog”) such as memory or concentration difficulties.  
   • Orthostatic intolerance (symptoms get worse when standing or sitting upright and improve when lying down).

2. Additional common symptoms  
   • Muscle or joint pain without swelling or redness.  
   • Headaches of a new type or severity.  
   • Sore throat, tender lymph nodes.  
   • Sensitivity to light, sound, or chemicals.  
   • Flu-like feelings, chills, night sweats.

3. Possible causes (still under study)  
   • Viral or other infections (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus, COVID-19).  
   • Immune-system dysregulation.  
   • Hormonal imbalances (e.g., low cortisol).  
   • Genetic and environmental factors.  
   No single cause has been proven; it may represent several overlapping sub-types.

4. Diagnosis  
   • Primarily clinical—based on symptom history and exclusion of other illnesses (thyroid disorders, anemia, sleep apnea, major depression, etc.).  
   • No definitive laboratory test yet, but doctors may run blood work, sleep studies, or autonomic testing to rule out other conditions.  
   • Diagnostic criteria: U.S. IOM/SEID 2015 or Canadian Consensus Criteria are often used.

5. Management and treatment  
   • Individualized energy-management strategies (pacing and activity management to avoid post-exertional crashes).  
   • Sleep optimization (good sleep hygiene, possible low-dose medications).  
   • Pain relief (NSAIDs, low-dose tricyclics, pregabalin, etc.).  
   • Addressing orthostatic intolerance (increased fluids/salt, compression garments, medications like fludrocortisone or midodrine).  
   • Cognitive-behavioral therapy can help some patients adapt and cope, but is not a cure.  
   • Gradual, carefully monitored activity therapy may help select patients, but over-exertion can worsen symptoms; newer guidelines emphasize caution with graded exercise.  
   • Treat co-existing problems (allergies, IBS, depression/anxiety) to improve overall quality of life.

6. Prognosis  
   • Course is variable; some experience partial improvement, others remain severely affected for years.  
   • Early diagnosis, symptom-targeted management, and pacing can improve functioning, but no universal cure exists yet.

7. Support resources  
   • U.S. CDC ME/CFS website  
   • Solve ME/CFS Initiative (solvecfs.org)  
   • ME Association (UK)  
   • Local or online support groups for coping strategies and shared experiences.
